sites.name: Shark & Yolanda Reef
sites.description: Signature Ras Mohammed drift running from Anemone City past Shark Reef to Yolanda, over two coral pinnacles with the wreck's cargo scattered on the sand and huge schools of snapper and jack. Currents are often strong and can shift or pulse downward without warning (especially in summer) -- get in fast so you don't drift on the surface and miss the wall, and stay alert for heavy boat traffic when you surface. The wall itself drops away to well over 700m, so this is a dive for confident, buoyancy-aware divers.
sites.pro_tip: The Yolanda wreck's cargo includes a row of seven British-standard toilets sitting on the shallow reef -- a favorite photo op, but the fire coral crowding around them is easy to brush against in a shorty wetsuit.

sites.name: Shark Observatory
sites.description: Sheer vertical wall right at the exposed tip of Ras Mohammed, dropping into open blue water; pelagic action, occasional reef and oceanic whitetip sharks, and cruising barracuda. Being the most exposed corner of the park it can pick up a stronger, more unpredictable current than the sheltered sites nearby, so it's usually reserved for divers comfortable in blue water with nothing below but depth.
sites.pro_tip: The name is a holdover from when sharks were reliably spotted from this promontory before mass tourism arrived in Sharm -- treat any shark sighting today as a bonus, not a guarantee.

sites.name: Anemone City
sites.description: Two pinnacles carpeted in magnificent anemones and Red Sea anemonefish, dived as a drift between two reef columns that's flushed by a strong current most of the time -- many boats treat it as the warm-up drift that feeds straight into Shark & Yolanda. Calm, current-free days are rare here, so a current check before entry is standard practice.

sites.name: Jackfish Alley
sites.description: Gentle drift dive through sandy alleys and a small cave swim-through packed with shoaling glassfish, with resident jacks, groupers and rays cruising the walls. Current is usually mild compared to Ras Mohammed's more exposed sites, making it a good option when the wind picks up elsewhere -- though the cave sections need decent buoyancy control to avoid silting out the glassfish clouds.
sites.pro_tip: Look for a white mark on the cliff face near the start of the dive -- it marks the cave entrance at about 5m that's thick with glassfish; whitetip reef sharks are often found napping on the sandy plateau nearby in the afternoon.

sites.name: Eel Garden
sites.description: Gentle sandy slope running from the fringing reef at around 12m down to a drop-off near 35m, home to a colony of the Red Sea's endemic garden eels swaying in the current -- approach slowly and stay low, as they retreat into their burrows at the first sign of a diver moving fast. An easy, low-current dive close to shore, but keep an eye on depth if you follow the slope toward the drop-off.

sites.name: Jackson Reef
sites.description: Northernmost Tiran reef, with schooling scalloped hammerheads on the northern plateau in summer and a wall of healthy hard coral. Currents run fast along the wall and the water between Jackson and neighbouring Woodhouse Reef has earned the nickname 'the washing machine' for currents that can hit from any direction -- the northern tip in particular can turn powerful with little warning, so this is a drift for experienced, current-comfortable divers only.
sites.pro_tip: Hammerheads are a morning game here -- they patrol the blue off the north side in the early hours before the day's boat traffic builds, and odds are best on an ebbing tide from July to September.

sites.name: Woodhouse Reef
sites.description: Long narrow drift reef with a saddle at its centre; eagle rays and reef sharks patrol the wall. There are no fixed moorings here so every dive is a drift, and the current often builds partway through -- best dived in calm weather with a guide who reads the direction before you jump in.
sites.pro_tip: The standout feature is a canyon opening around 30m on the northern half of the eastern side -- worth the detour if you're certified for the depth, but currents at the northern tip can turn strong with little warning.

sites.name: Thomas Reef
sites.description: Smallest of the Tiran reefs but arguably the prettiest, with a spectacular soft coral canyon and plateau on a fast drift. Current here can turn very strong with little notice and change direction mid-dive, so plan for a boat pickup rather than trying to swim back -- good air consumption helps if you want to linger in the canyon.
sites.pro_tip: The gorgonian sea fan forest spreads across the plateau at about 25m, just before the canyon drop -- a good spot to pause and regroup before committing to the drift.

sites.name: Gordon Reef
sites.description: Southernmost Tiran reef, marked by the wreck of the Loullia freighter on the reef plate; a natural shark amphitheatre and resident turtles on the sandy plateau. Current can be tricky and unpredictable around the reef's corners, and the site is only reliably diveable in calm weather with little wind -- ask about conditions before committing to the deeper plateau.
sites.pro_tip: Keep an eye on the shallow southern plateau for eagle rays, and in spring, the occasional manta passing over the same ground.

sites.name: Ras Umm Sid
sites.description: Iconic gorgonian forest wall right off Sharm, with easy shore or boat access and some of the best pelagic action of any local site. Current is usually mild enough for a relaxed mooring dive, but it can pick up unpredictably on the northern corner of the reef -- if that happens it's harder to get back to the exit point, so keep track of the current direction throughout.
sites.pro_tip: Watch the far corner where currents meet -- schools of snapper and barracuda stack up there, and it's the spot locals watch for the rare passing whale shark or manta when the current picks up.

sites.name: The Temple
sites.description: Three pinnacles sheltered close to shore, starting shallow around 6m before a tiny swim-through opens onto the blue where the wall drops past 30m for those who want to go deeper. Usually calm and sheltered, which is exactly why it's a classic night dive and training site, full of glassfish and lionfish hunting under torchlight.
sites.pro_tip: On a night dive, keep your torch beam soft and indirect on the basket stars -- direct light makes them contract into a tight ball, while indirect light lets them stay fanned open to feed.

sites.name: The Tower
sites.description: Dramatic canyon and wall in central-south Sharm dropping well past 60m, its face covered in soft coral and clouds of glassfish. Recreational divers stay well above the true depth of the canyon, but it's easy to get target-fixated on the wall and go deeper than planned, so watch your computer -- current is usually gentle but can build if the wind is up.
sites.pro_tip: Only one of the Tower's two cracks should be swum through -- the other is lined with delicate gorgonians that are easily damaged by fins, so stick to the wider, sandier crack.

sites.name: Far Garden
sites.description: The furthest and least crowded of the three Na'ama garden bays, reached from the Reef Oasis and Sharm Plaza pontoons; coral heads, moray eels and the occasional turtle over a gently sloping sandy bay. Generally calm and sheltered with only mild current, though the coral gets noticeably healthier the further you swim from the pontoons and the crowds.
sites.pro_tip: The small coral 'ergs' scattered near the top of the drop-off are a better place to hover and wait than the main reef wall -- passing pelagics tend to swing past them first.

sites.name: SS Thistlegorm
sites.description: Legendary WWII cargo wreck in the Strait of Gubal, its holds still packed with trucks, motorbikes and a locomotive on deck; huge schools of batfish and barracuda patrol the wreck. Currents in the open water here can be punishing with nothing to hide behind mid-water, so most boats run a descent/ascent line -- stick to it. It's also one of Egypt's busiest sites, with day boats converging between 8-10am, so a liveaboard's early-morning or night dive slot is far calmer than the midday rush.
sites.pro_tip: If you're not on a liveaboard's dawn slot, an early-afternoon dive (after 2pm, once day-trip boats start heading back to Sharm) is the next-best window for calmer holds and settled silt.

sites.name: Dunraven (Sara H)
sites.description: Victorian-era steamship wreck sitting in about 30m at the southern end of Sha'ab Mahmoud (Beacon Rock), broken in two and completely upside-down on the sand; swim-throughs thick with glassfish and resident morays. It's a sheltered, relatively easy wreck dive by Red Sea standards -- some chop can build on the surface, but conditions inside the hull are usually calm. The open back section is penetrable for those with wreck training, though as with any overhead environment, fin carefully to avoid stirring up silt.
sites.pro_tip: Stick to external exploration on a first visit -- the interior is silty, dark and disorienting without wreck training, even though multiple penetration points exist.

sites.name: Ras Nasrani
sites.description: Varied wall and coral plateau about 11km north of Naama Bay, thick with gorgonian fans; can be dived as a drift, semi-drift or calm mooring dive depending on conditions. When the current is running it can turn seriously strong on the reef's corner, and that version of the dive is best left to experienced drift divers with solid air consumption and good current-diving fitness.

sites.name: Near Garden
sites.description: Closest of the northern Naama Bay gardens, just around the headland from Naama itself -- a gently sloping sandy bay dotted with coral heads and a favorite for bluespotted rays. Almost always calm and current-free, which makes it popular for relaxed afternoon dives, though the coral nearest the entry points shows the wear of heavy day-boat traffic.
sites.pro_tip: A good night-dive pick -- blue-spotted stingrays tend to settle on the sandy ledge after dark, and it's one of the few local sites that also gets occasional grey reef shark passes off the headland.

sites.name: Middle Garden
sites.description: Large, sheltered sandy bay and the most popular of the three garden bays -- very protected from weather and about as current-free as Sharm diving gets, making it an ideal first-holiday-dive or Discover Scuba site. Coral cover is thinner in the busy central section near the pontoons, but improves noticeably along the quieter, deeper edges of the bay.

sites.name: Ras Katy
sites.description: Sharm's southernmost local dive site, a sheltered pinnacle and drop-off just off the marina at Sharm el-Mina; schools of fusiliers around the main pinnacle and clownfish tucked into anemones. Usually calm and shallow -- a regular pick for courses, check dives and night dives -- though current can build toward the corner facing Temple, so confirm direction with your guide. A resident whitetip reef shark holds around 28m on the drop-off (which itself plunges past 70m) for those who want to extend the dive deeper.
sites.pro_tip: From the plateau heading toward Temple, look for eagle rays, fantails and even the occasional manta cruising the pinnacles -- and check the SE ridge at 22m for shoals of red-toothed triggerfish, bannerfish and sometimes tuna.

sites.name: Ras Ghozlani
sites.description: One of the first sites inside Ras Mohammed National Park, at the entrance to Marsa Bareika bay; a gentle drift over pristine hard coral gardens down to a sandy plateau and drop-off near 25m. Current here is rarely strong compared to the park's more exposed walls, best dived in the morning when the sun lights up the reef -- a good, calmer alternative when Shark & Yolanda's current is running hard. Keep an eye on the sand and rubble for octopus and other hard-to-find critters.
sites.pro_tip: During summer, keep half an eye on the blue past the drop-off -- this gentle bay corner gets occasional whale shark and sailfish passes that most divers miss because they're focused on the reef itself.

sites.name: Amphoras
sites.description: Named for the wreckage of a centuries-old vessel that sank here carrying a cargo of amphoras, whose broken remains still lie encrusted in coral behind one of the site's pinnacles; a fringing reef wall to about 10m gives way to a long sandy slope down to a 25-30m drop-off. Turtles, stingrays and lionfish are regular sightings along the slope. Suited to most levels in calm conditions, but current can build as you approach the drop-off, so watch depth and air if you're drifting along the wall.
sites.pro_tip: Ask your guide to include Turtle Bay, the slope between Amphoras and neighbouring Paradise dropping from 9m to 25m -- it's a more reliable place to find turtles than the amphora wreckage itself.

sites.name: Kormoran Wreck
sites.description: A merchant ship that ran aground on the north side of Laguna Reef, Tiran, in 1984 -- it sits in less than 12m with its stern breaking the surface, propeller, winch and engine still visible and table corals colonizing the hull. Abundant sohal surgeonfish patrol the shallows. Easy, all-levels wreck diving, but it's only safely diveable on a calm day; swell at this shallow, exposed depth can make entries and exits hazardous, so it's best dived on the afternoon tide change when the current eases.
sites.pro_tip: The nearby Zingara wreck lies close by too -- ask about combining both wrecks in one dive if conditions allow, since Kormoran alone is a short, shallow dive.

sites.name: Laguna Reef
sites.description: A shallow coral lagoon on the west side of Tiran Island itself, split into North and South Laguna by a hard coral wall; a drift along the outer wall between the Laguna entrance and the green beacon, with schools of butterflyfish along the wall and glassfish-covered pinnacles draped in gorgonian fans. Strong tidal currents dictate which direction you'll dive, so it's usually planned for the afternoon when the flow eases -- ask your guide which way the tide is running before you jump in. Sits close to the Kormoran wreck on the reef's northern edge.

sites.name: White Knight
sites.description: A wide bay north of Naama Bay near Ras Nasrani, centered on an open canyon that cuts through the reef from about 8m down to a sandy gully with swim-throughs at 10m and 35m; hard coral walls, a resident garden eel colony, and the broken, upturned hull of a dive boat lost in 1994 sheltering groupers and triggerfish. A versatile, fairly benign dive suited to most levels, though the gully's depth range demands attention to your computer, and the occasional manta ray has been sighted cruising through the bay.

sites.name: Ras Hootch
sites.description: A lesser-known local spot just next to The Temple, reaching about 30m. Not documented by dive operators or online sources -- added from a diver's own first-hand knowledge of the site rather than published references.

species.description: The world's largest fish, a gentle plankton-feeding giant. A rare summer visitor to the Sharm reefs and open water off Tiran.
species.population_info: Endangered globally; population has declined over 50% in recent decades due to fishing and vessel strikes, though exact numbers are unknown. Sightings around Sharm are rare, seasonal visitors.

species.description: Schooling hammerheads gather on Tiran's northern plateaus in summer; an unmistakable silhouette and a bucket-list encounter.
species.habitat: Deep reef plateaus and blue water
species.population_info: Critically Endangered; heavily depleted worldwide by shark-fin fishing, with some regional populations down over 90%. The Red Sea retains one of the last reliable schooling sites.

species.description: Bold, curious open-water shark with rounded white-tipped fins; most often seen off exposed offshore reefs.
species.population_info: Critically Endangered; global numbers have collapsed by an estimated 80-95% since the 1990s due to longline fishing, making Red Sea sightings increasingly rare.

species.description: Classic requiem shark patrolling the deeper reef walls and drop-offs of Ras Mohammed and Tiran.
species.population_info: Endangered range-wide from overfishing, but resident populations in Ras Mohammed's protected waters remain comparatively healthy.

species.description: Slender reef shark that rests on the sand under coral ledges by day; identifiable by white-tipped dorsal and tail.
species.population_info: Vulnerable to overfishing due to very slow reproduction, but still commonly encountered resting on reef ledges by day in protected areas.

species.description: Huge, inquisitive humphead wrasse with maze-like face markings; the friendly giant of the Red Sea reef.
species.population_info: Endangered globally, mainly from the live reef fish trade in parts of Asia; Red Sea individuals are protected and this remains one of the more reliable places to see large adults.

species.description: Beautiful reef turtle with a serrated shell, seen grazing on soft coral and sponges across the gardens.
species.population_info: Critically Endangered; an estimated 20,000–23,000 nesting females remain worldwide after centuries of tortoiseshell trade decimated populations.

species.description: Large herbivorous turtle grazing on seagrass; rounder head than the hawksbill.
species.population_info: Endangered globally, though considerably more numerous than the hawksbill; the Red Sea hosts resident feeding populations that graze the seagrass beds and reef gardens.

species.description: Vivid electric-blue-spotted stingray tucked under coral ledges and in sandy pockets.
species.population_info: Least Concern and one of the most frequently seen rays in the Indo-Pacific; population trend is stable across most of its range.

species.description: The Red Sea's largest moray, mouth agape as it breathes; often paired with cleaner wrasse.
species.population_info: Least Concern and widespread across the Indo-Pacific; no population counts exist, but it's one of the most reliably encountered morays on Red Sea reefs.

species.description: Superbly camouflaged flathead lying motionless on sand and rubble, with ornate lacy eye lappets.
species.population_info: Least Concern; considered common throughout its range, though its camouflage means it's likely seen far less often than it's actually present.

species.description: Elegant, venomous ambush predator with fanned pectoral rays; abundant on night dives.
species.population_info: Least Concern and abundant throughout its native Red Sea and Indo-Pacific range, where -- unlike its invasive Atlantic populations -- it plays its natural role in the reef ecosystem.

species.description: The Red Sea's endemic two-bar clownfish, darting among the tentacles of its host anemone.
species.population_info: Least Concern; a Red Sea endemic found wherever its host anemones grow, with populations considered stable and abundant.

species.description: Stunning blue-and-yellow striped angelfish; juveniles wear concentric blue rings.
species.population_info: Least Concern and common across the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea; population trend is stable.

species.description: Vividly banded orange, blue and white angelfish that hugs coral cover.
species.population_info: Least Concern; found across the Indo-Pacific, generally in lower densities than other angelfish but not considered threatened.

species.description: Elegant black-white-yellow banded fish with a long trailing dorsal filament, often in pairs.
species.population_info: Least Concern; a Red Sea endemic that's abundant on nearly every reef, often seen drifting in pairs.

species.description: Golden yellow Red Sea endemic butterflyfish with a blue-grey eye mask; drifts in pairs under table corals.
species.population_info: Least Concern; another Red Sea endemic, common and easily recognized by its golden color and blue eye mask.

species.description: Boldly painted Red Sea trigger with a striking face mask; shy and quick to bolt into holes.
species.population_info: Least Concern; endemic to the Red Sea and common on sandy reef flats, though quick to dart for cover.

species.description: The reef's bulldozer; large and territorial, especially when guarding a nest — give it space.
species.population_info: Least Concern and widespread across the Indo-Pacific; the reef's largest triggerfish and a formidable nest-guarder.

species.description: Clouds of orange and pink anthias hovering over every coral head — the wallpaper of the Red Sea.
species.population_info: Least Concern and extremely abundant -- forms some of the densest fish aggregations on any Red Sea reef.

species.description: Bright yellow schooling snapper with blue stripes, massing around coral heads and the Yolanda wreck.
species.population_info: Least Concern and abundant across the Indo-Pacific, often massing in large schools around wrecks and reef structure.

species.description: Silver jacks that form dense, slow-swirling schools on the reef edge, best at Shark & Yolanda.
species.population_info: Least Concern; forms large, swirling schools that are a signature sight at current-swept sites like Shark & Yolanda Reef.

species.description: Solitary silver ambush predator hanging in the current with a menacing jaw of teeth.
species.population_info: Least Concern and found throughout tropical seas worldwide; usually encountered solo, hanging motionless in the current.

species.description: Huge red nudibranch that 'dances' by flexing its mantle when swimming; a prized night-dive find.
species.population_info: Not formally assessed for conservation status, but considered common throughout the Indo-Pacific; most often found on night dives.

species.description: Brilliant red-orange grouper flecked with blue spots, perched on coral watching the reef.
species.population_info: Least Concern and one of the most commonly encountered groupers on Red Sea reefs.

species.description: Endearing Red Sea endemic puffer with a dark mask around the eyes, hovering over the reef.
species.population_info: Least Concern; a Red Sea endemic seen on almost every reef dive in the region.

species.description: Small, distinctive black-tipped fins cutting through the shallows; often seen patrolling shallow reef flats and lagoons.
species.population_info: Vulnerable due to slow reproduction and widespread coastal fishing pressure across its range, though shallow reef flats in protected areas still host regular sightings.

species.description: Elegant white-spotted ray gliding over the sandy plateau on Gordon Reef's southwest corner, sometimes in small formations.
species.population_info: Endangered; global populations have declined significantly from targeted and incidental ray fisheries, making Red Sea sightings a genuinely special encounter.

species.description: Enormous, graceful filter-feeder with a wingspan up to 4.5m; a rare, unforgettable visitor to Tiran's plateaus.
species.population_info: Vulnerable; produces at most one pup every few years, making populations slow to recover from fishing pressure elsewhere in its range. Sightings around Tiran are rare and opportunistic rather than reliably seasonal.

species.description: Tiny, cryptic seahorse that clings to soft coral and seagrass with its tail; a genuine find that takes a sharp eye.
species.population_info: Vulnerable; like most seahorses, population numbers are poorly documented, but habitat loss and collection for traditional medicine and the aquarium trade are recognized threats across its range.

species.description: Rounded electric ray that lies half-buried in sand, capable of a startling electric shock if disturbed.
species.population_info: Not formally assessed; poorly studied like most electric rays, but considered uncommon rather than rare on Red Sea sand flats.

species.description: Striking black-and-white honeycomb-patterned moray, often seen with its head poking from a reef crevice.
species.population_info: Least Concern and widespread across the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea; the region's largest moray after the giant moray.

species.description: Large, colorful Red Sea wrasse with a distinctive fan-shaped tail, cruising over open reef.
species.population_info: Near Threatened; populations have declined in parts of its range from spearfishing, though it remains regularly seen on Red Sea reefs.

species.description: Large angelfish with a bold yellow bar and blue-black body, a common but always striking reef resident.
species.population_info: Least Concern and common across the Red Sea and western Indian Ocean.

species.description: Unmistakable polka-dotted black-and-white triggerfish with a yellow-ringed mouth; an occasional deeper-reef surprise.
species.population_info: Least Concern globally, though less commonly seen on Red Sea reefs than in other parts of the Indo-Pacific -- an aquarium-trade favorite that's a real treat to spot wild.

species.description: Tall, disc-shaped, curious fish that often approaches divers around wrecks and pinnacles.
species.population_info: Least Concern; common around wrecks and pinnacles throughout the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea.

species.description: Boxy, horned little fish that hovers shyly over sand and rubble, a favorite macro subject.
species.population_info: Least Concern and found throughout the Indo-Pacific; juveniles are more frequently seen than the shyer adults.

species.description: Master of camouflage, changing color and texture in an instant; mostly nocturnal and a real prize to spot.
species.population_info: Not formally assessed for conservation status; short-lived and fast-growing like most octopuses, with populations that can fluctuate seasonally.

species.description: Lumpy, sponge-like ambush predator that lures prey with a rod-like fin and can swallow fish nearly its own size in an instant; expert camouflage makes it a real find.
species.habitat: Reef and rubble, often near sponges
species.population_info: Least Concern; uncommon to encounter simply because its camouflage is so effective, not because it's genuinely rare.

species.description: Dazzlingly colored burrow-dweller with club-like claws that strike faster than any other animal on Earth; a favorite macro sighting.
species.population_info: Not formally assessed for conservation status; common in its burrows across the Indo-Pacific, though its secretive habits make it an infrequent sighting.

species.description: Fast, vividly green-and-pink wrasse darting constantly over shallow reef; one of the most common fish you'll see.
species.population_info: Least Concern and extremely abundant -- one of the very first fish you'll notice on almost any shallow Red Sea reef.

species.description: Comically cube-shaped fish, bright yellow with dark spots as a juvenile, that swims with tiny fins in a slow hover.
species.population_info: Least Concern and common throughout the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea; juveniles' bright yellow fades with age.

species.description: Bold, territorial Red Sea surgeonfish with electric blue-and-black striping, fiercely guarding its patch of shallow reef.
species.population_info: Least Concern; a Red Sea and Gulf of Aden specialty, extremely common and fiercely territorial on shallow reef flats.

species.description: Vividly banded blue-green lobster with striped legs and a violet tail fan, wedged into reef crevices by day and most active on night dives.
species.population_info: Least Concern and widespread across the Indo-Pacific including the Red Sea; nocturnal and solitary, so daytime finds are down to luck spotting antennae poking from an overhang.

species.description: Intelligent, fast-changing squid that hovers in small schools over reef tops and sandy flats, flashing rippling color patterns; easiest to approach at dusk.
species.habitat: Reef edges and sandy flats near the surface
species.population_info: Not formally assessed by the IUCN; short-lived (roughly a year) with fast population turnover, so sightings vary by season rather than long-term decline.
species.best_season: Year-round (most active at dusk and night)

species.description: A powerful, solitary pelagic hunter that patrols steep drop-offs and current-swept walls, often glimpsed cruising at the edge of visibility.
species.population_info: Least Concern overall, but as a top reef predator its local appearances are tied to strong current and season; most reliable in summer when it moves onto the Tiran reefs and Ras Mohammed's walls to feed.

species.description: Resident pods frequently bow-ride dive boats crossing the Straits of Tiran, with a stockier build and shorter beak than other Red Sea dolphins.
species.habitat: Open channel water and reef-adjacent seas
species.population_info: Least Concern globally; a resident pod inhabits the Straits of Tiran and is a near-daily sight for boats crossing to Jackson and Woodhouse reefs.

species.description: The Red Sea's dominant large cuttlefish, hovering motionless over sand and rubble with a W-shaped pupil, capable of near-instant color and pattern changes.
species.population_info: Data Deficient on the IUCN Red List due to sparse population monitoring; widely distributed across the Indo-Pacific and one of the most intelligent invertebrates divers regularly encounter in the Red Sea.

species.description: Larger, grayish puffer covered in fine white spots that radiate into rings around the eyes and pectoral fins, distinct from the smaller, dark-masked Red Sea endemic puffer sharing the same reefs.
species.habitat: Reef slopes, lagoons and sandy bays
species.population_info: Least Concern and widespread across the Indo-Pacific including the Red Sea; commonly seen hovering alone over reef and sand.

species.description: Also called the cowtail stingray, a broad, dark-backed ray with a distinctive fin-like fold running along its long whip tail, usually found half-buried in sand in sheltered bays.
species.population_info: Near Threatened, with suspected ongoing population declines from fishing pressure across its Indo-Pacific range (targeted for its leather-quality skin); still a regular find in Sharm's sheltered sandy bays.

species.description: Unlike the solitary Great Barracuda, this species forms large schooling 'tornadoes' over reef walls and drop-offs, marked by dark chevron bands along its flanks.
species.habitat: Reef walls and drop-offs, schooling in open water
species.population_info: Least Concern; schools can range from a few dozen to several hundred individuals and move between sites, so sightings depend on where the school currently is.

species.description: A small but vividly striped blue, yellow and black sea slug, one of the most commonly photographed nudibranchs on Red Sea reefs, usually found grazing on its preferred red sponge.
species.population_info: Not formally assessed for conservation status; described from the Red Sea, where it remains one of the most frequently recorded nudibranchs.

species.description: The most venomous fish in the sea, camouflaged as an encrusted rock or lump of rubble on the seabed; easy to swim right past, and just as easy to accidentally kneel on, so watch where you put your hands and fins.
species.population_info: Least Concern and widely distributed across the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea; its perfect camouflage makes it far more common than the rarity of actual sightings suggests.
